name: Design a URL Shortener
intent: Turn long links into short ones that redirect quickly, and grow the design from one server to millions of redirects per second.
finalIntro: One redirect through everything built above.
prompt: Design a service like bit.ly. A user pastes a long URL and gets a short link such as sho.rt/aZ3k9Q. Anyone who opens the short link is redirected to the original URL.
functional: Create a short link for a long URL
Redirect a short link to its long URL
Optional: custom aliases and an expiry date
nonFunctional: Redirects must be fast (under about 50 ms on the server) because users wait for them
Reading is far more common than writing: assume 100 redirects for every new link
Available: a dead short link breaks every page that embeds it
A short code must never point at two different URLs
Codes should not reveal how many links exist or the order they were made in

firstAttempt.text: One web server and one database. The database has a table of (short code, long URL). Creating a link inserts a row. Following a link looks the row up and replies with a redirect (HTTP 301 means moved permanently, 302 means moved temporarily). It works, and it is the right start for a small product.
limits: One machine is the only way in: if it stops, everything stops
Every redirect hits the database, so read traffic limits the whole service
All data lives on one disk, which fills up one day
Nothing stops one client from creating millions of links
Counting clicks adds a database write to every redirect

steps.title: Many app servers behind a load balancer
steps.problem: A single server tops out at roughly a thousand redirects per second and is a single point of failure.
steps.fix: Keep the app servers stateless (they hold no data of their own) and put a load balancer in front. Add servers as traffic grows, and replace any server that fails, because the balancer stops sending it requests.
steps.tradeoff: Gains capacity and availability for the app tier. The database is now one shared dependency that every server hits, so it becomes the next bottleneck.

steps.title: Index the short code
steps.problem: Each redirect looks up a row by its short code. Without an index the database scans the whole table, which gets slower as links accumulate.
steps.fix: Make the short code the primary key (or add a unique index on it). A lookup then walks a small tree instead of reading every row, and the unique index also guarantees that one code never maps to two URLs.
steps.tradeoff: Reads become fast and codes stay unique, at the cost of a little extra storage and a slightly slower insert.

steps.title: Cache the hot links
steps.problem: With 100 reads per write, a small share of popular links gets most of the traffic, yet each redirect still queries the database.
steps.fix: Put a cache such as Redis (a fast in-memory store) between the app servers and the database. On a miss, read from the database and store the result. A link's target almost never changes, so entries can live for hours.
steps.tradeoff: The database sees only the misses, often under a tenth of the traffic. In return you must handle expiry, deleted or edited links, and a cold cache after a restart.

steps.title: Replicate the database for reads and failover
steps.problem: Cache misses plus all writes still land on one database, and if it dies the service has no data.
steps.fix: Keep the primary (the copy that takes writes) and add read replicas (copies that serve reads) for cache misses. A replica can be promoted if the primary fails.
steps.tradeoff: More read capacity and a recovery path. A newly created link may not be on a replica yet, so the app should read a fresh link from the primary, or handle a brief not-found.

steps.title: Shard when the data outgrows one machine
steps.problem: Billions of links over several years will not fit on one disk, and one primary cannot take unlimited writes.
steps.fix: Split the table across shards by short code, using consistent hashing so a lookup knows which shard to ask and adding a shard moves only a small share of keys. Each shard keeps its own replicas.
steps.tradeoff: Storage and write capacity scale out. Queries across all links (for example, every link of one user) become harder, and resharding needs care.

steps.title: Rate limit link creation
steps.problem: Spammers and buggy scripts create millions of links, filling storage and burning short codes.
steps.fix: Limit requests per API key or IP at the edge, before they reach the app. Return 429 with a Retry-After header to clients that exceed the limit.
steps.tradeoff: Protects capacity and storage, but a limit set too low blocks real users, and a shared IP can punish a whole office.

steps.title: Count clicks off the critical path
steps.problem: Writing a click to the database during every redirect makes redirects slower and ties their speed to the analytics store.
steps.fix: The app server publishes a small click event to a queue and redirects immediately. A worker reads the queue and updates the counters in batches, and a slow or failed worker only delays the numbers.
steps.tradeoff: Redirects stay fast and decoupled. Counts become slightly delayed and, with at-least-once delivery (an event can arrive twice), may include duplicates unless the worker is idempotent.

failures.scenario: The cache cluster restarts and is empty
failures.impact: Every redirect misses and goes to the database at once, which can overload it (a cache stampede).
failures.answer: Warm the cache before sending it traffic, allow only one request per link to refill an entry, and keep the database able to survive a spike or shed excess load.

failures.impact: Links on that shard cannot be resolved, so roughly one in N redirects fails.
failures.answer: Each shard has replicas, so one is promoted. While that happens, the cache keeps serving popular links, and a circuit breaker makes the rest fail fast instead of tying up app servers.

failures.scenario: The analytics worker falls hours behind
failures.impact: Click counts are stale, but nobody is redirected more slowly.
failures.answer: This is the point of the queue. Watch queue depth and age, add workers, and bound the queue so it cannot grow without limit. Redirects never depended on it.

alternatives.title: How to create the short code

options.name: Counter encoded in base62 (digits and letters)
options.pro: Never collides, short codes, trivial to implement
options.con: Sequential codes are guessable, and a single counter must be shared or split among servers

options.name: Hash of the long URL, truncated
options.pro: The same URL always gives the same code, with no counter to coordinate
options.con: Truncation causes collisions that must be detected and retried

options.name: Random code, checked against the database
options.con: Needs a uniqueness check on every insert, and collisions rise as the table fills

alternatives.pick: A counter, scrambled with a reversible multiplication and encoded in base62: unique by construction and not obviously sequential (this hides the order, it is not security). See the code below.

alternatives.title: Which redirect status to use

options.name: 301 Moved Permanently
options.pro: Browsers cache it, so repeat visits skip your servers entirely
options.con: Cached redirects cannot be changed or counted, so you lose click analytics and the ability to edit or disable a link

options.name: 302 Found (temporary)
options.pro: Every visit reaches your service, so you can count it and change the target

alternatives.pick: 302 when you need analytics or editable links, 301 when you want the least load and the links are permanent.

alternatives.title: SQL or NoSQL for the links table

options.name: Relational database
options.pro: Familiar, unique constraints and transactions come built in

options.name: Key-value or wide-column store
options.pro: Sharding and replication are built in, and lookups by key are exactly what it does best
options.con: Weaker constraints, so uniqueness of codes needs care

alternatives.pick: The access pattern is one lookup by key, so either works. Start relational for simplicity, and move to a key-value store when sharding becomes the main concern.

roles.label: Edge
roles.description: Entry points that shield the system: load balancer and rate limiter.

roles.label: Async
roles.description: Queues and the workers that read them.

quiz.question: Redirects take 15 ms. After the team adds an UPDATE that raises a click counter on the link row during every redirect, p99 (the time that 99% of redirects beat) grows to 120 ms, and the most popular links are the slowest. How should clicks be counted?
options: Add read replicas and send the counter updates to whichever replica has the lowest load at that moment
Publish a small click event to a queue and redirect at once, with a worker adding counts in batches
Add an index on the clicks column so that the update can find the row to change more quickly
Add more app servers, so each one handles fewer of the redirects that update the counter
quiz.explanation: The redirect should not wait for analytics, and a queue lets a worker batch many clicks into one write. Replicas cannot take writes. More servers send even more updates to the same hot rows, and an index on a changing column makes each update slower.

quiz.question: Product wants a click count for every link and the ability to disable an abusive link within a minute. About 100 redirects happen per link created, and the team also wants low load. Which redirect status should the service return?
options: 301, because browsers cache it and cut the load, and click counts can be taken from the access logs
301, and purge the CDN cache when a link is disabled, which also clears any copies cached in browsers
302, so every visit reaches the service, which counts it and can change the target
301 for new links, switching to 302 only after a link has received its first abuse report
quiz.explanation: A 302 is not cached, so every visit can be counted and the target can change at once. A browser that cached a 301 never contacts the service again, so those visits are missing from logs and a disabled link keeps working for them. A CDN purge cannot reach browser caches. Switching to 302 only after an abuse report is too late for browsers that already cached the 301.

quiz.question: Redirects run at 10,000 per second with a 95% cache hit rate, so the database sees 500 reads per second and can serve about 2,000. The cache cluster restarts and comes back empty. What happens, and which step helps most?
options: Most redirects miss and overload the database, so warm the cache and let one request refill each link
The database copes, since primary key lookups are fast, and the cache refills in a few seconds on its own
Misses jump, so make the app servers retry failed lookups three times at once to ride out the spike
Misses jump, so raise every cache TTL (time to live, how long an entry is kept) to 24 hours, which stops the database from seeing the load
quiz.explanation: With an empty cache every redirect is a miss, so the database gets 10,000 reads per second, five times what it can serve, and fast key lookups do not change that. Warming plus one refill per key (request coalescing) keeps the load near the real number of distinct links. Instant retries multiply the load, and a longer TTL does nothing for entries that are not there yet.
